root/riboviria/orthornavirae/negarnaviri.name: Orthobunyavirus
root/riboviria/orthornavirae/negarnaviri.note: The largest genus of arboviruses. Species are grouped into serogroups (Simbu, California, Bunyamwera, Group C, Guamá, Capim and others). Human pathogenicity is highly uneven: a handful of species cause well-defined disease (Oropouche fever, La Crosse encephalitis), many are known only from serosurveys, and some are purely veterinary teratogens (Akabane, Schmallenberg). Because serogroup antibodies cross-react, species-level attribution usually requires sequencing or neutralisation.

evidence: Hundreds of neuroinvasive cases confirmed by CSF serology under US national arboviral surveillance each decade.

profile.headline: Simbu-serogroup orthobunyavirus of the Manzanilla clade, maintained in pigs and Culicoides biting midges across East and South Asia. Known mainly from swine serosurveys and vector surveillance; a single 2026 report describes severe human disease.
profile.syndrome: Human disease is documented from a single published case: a 2026 New England Journal of Medicine report of severe hepatitis, enteritis and coagulopathy. Beyond that the human evidence is serological — IgG in people in Vietnam and in two individuals in Karnataka, India — so the clinical spectrum, including whether mild or self-limiting illness is common, is genuinely unknown. No neuroinvasive human case has been published, despite the neuropathogenicity of related simbuviruses.
profile.transmission: Arboviral, with Culicoides biting midges the likely vectors: most isolates come from midges, and experimental competence in mosquitoes is poor. Pigs act as amplifying hosts. Culex mosquitoes yield field isolates and support replication, but in oral-challenge experiments Cx. pipiens pallens reached only 4.8% dissemination and 0% transmission, so a mosquito-borne cycle is not established.
vectors: Culicoides spp. (biting midges) — the source of most isolates
Culex spp. — field isolates reported; experimental transmission not demonstrated
profile.reservoir: Domestic pigs (high seroprevalence), with birds also implicated; antibodies reported in cattle and sheep.
profile.geography: Vietnam, southern China (Yunnan, Hunan, Hainan, Guangdong), India (Karnataka, Maharashtra). Serological signal in Indian swine and humans.
profile.diagnosis: Virus-specific S-segment RT-qPCR (95% limit of detection 0.80 PFU/mL for the published OYAV primer/probe set), virus isolation in BHK-21, MA104 or PK15 cells, neutralisation and IgG ELISA. Not covered by routine arbovirus panels — requires targeted testing.
profile.management: Supportive only. No licensed antiviral or vaccine.
profile.prevention: Vector avoidance; midge and mosquito control around pig husbandry; surveillance of swine herds.
evidence: Isolated from Culex mosquitoes and pigs in Vietnam and China; isolate HN1304M recovered from Culicoides midges in Hunan (2013).
Oya virus isolate SZC50 from Yunnan midges killed suckling and IFN-α/β-receptor-deficient mice and induced CPE in three mammalian cell lines, demonstrating mammalian virulence.
>30% neutralising-antibody seroprevalence in Yunnan pigs (up to 95% in Malipo), establishing intense mammalian circulation.
Indian preparedness study screened human and swine sera by RT-PCR and anti-CQV IgG ELISA and found IgG in two people in Karnataka — the only human serological signal reported outside Vietnam.
Cat Que and Balagodu viruses isolated from a jungle myna and a paddy bird in Karnataka, India — Manzanilla clade, suggesting under-reported human and livestock infection.
Detected in Hainan biting midges 2019–2023 at a minimum infection rate of 0.4/1000.
Oya virus was isolated from Karnataka, India in 2016 and characterised as a Simbu-serogroup virus, independently of the Vietnamese and Chinese isolates.

Vector-competence testing of four mosquito species found Cx. pipiens pallens had the highest infection rate (40%) but a dissemination rate of 4.8% and a transmission rate of 0% — evidence against, not for, mosquito-borne transmission.
2026 NEJM case report: severe hepatitis, enteritis and coagulopathy attributed to Oya virus — the only published human case.
Mechanistic work shows OYAV (with Ebinur Lake virus) activates the AhR–CYP1A1 axis to suppress type I interferon responses — a defined immune-evasion module.

profile.headline: The most important human pathogen of the Simbu serogroup and, after dengue, one of the most frequent arboviral febrile illnesses in the Amazon basin. Major expansion across the Americas from 2023–2024.
profile.syndrome: Abrupt febrile illness ('Oropouche fever') with severe headache, myalgia, arthralgia, chills, photophobia and nausea; frequently relapsing after a few days of apparent recovery. Aseptic meningitis and meningoencephalitis occur. Vertical transmission with fetal loss and congenital anomalies reported during the 2024 expansion, as well as rare fatalities.
profile.transmission: Urban/peri-urban cycle via the biting midge Culicoides paraensis; sylvatic cycle involving mosquitoes. Vertical (mother-to-fetus) transmission documented.
profile.reservoir: Sylvatic cycle in non-human primates, sloths (Bradypus) and birds; humans amplify the urban cycle.
profile.geography: Amazon basin — Brazil, Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia, Panama, Trinidad; marked 2024 expansion including Cuba and travel-associated cases exported to Europe and North America.
profile.diagnosis: RT-PCR on acute serum (first ~5 days), IgM/IgG ELISA, virus isolation. Clinically indistinguishable from dengue — co-circulation demands specific testing.
profile.management: Supportive. Avoid NSAIDs until dengue is excluded. No specific antiviral.
profile.prevention: Midge control is difficult (C. paraensis is tiny and bites outdoors by day); fine-mesh screening, repellents, reduction of peridomestic breeding (decaying banana/cacao debris).
evidence: Repeatedly isolated from blood of febrile patients since the 1955 Trinidad index case; hundreds of thousands of cases in documented epidemics.
Reassortant members of the same species (Iquitos, Madre de Dios viruses) also recovered from human febrile cases in Peru and Venezuela.
2024 expansion produced the first well-documented deaths and vertically transmitted fetal infections.

profile.headline: Prototype orthobunyavirus. Its reassortant member Ngari virus (Bunyamwera backbone with Batai M segment) causes haemorrhagic fever in East Africa.
profile.syndrome: Bunyamwera and Germiston viruses: self-limiting fever with headache, rash and arthralgia. Ngari virus: documented haemorrhagic fever outbreaks in Kenya and Somalia, originally mistaken for Rift Valley fever.
profile.transmission: Mosquito-borne (Aedes, Anopheles, Culex).
profile.reservoir: Rodents and other small mammals; vertebrate hosts incompletely defined.
profile.geography: Sub-Saharan Africa; Xingu virus in South America.
profile.diagnosis: RT-PCR and serology; segment-level sequencing is required to recognise reassortants such as Ngari.
evidence: Bunyamwera virus isolated from humans and mosquitoes in Uganda (1943) — the genus prototype and the standard laboratory model.
Ngari virus recovered from haemorrhagic fever patients during the 1997–1998 East African outbreak, demonstrating that orthobunyavirus reassortment can create new human pathogens.

refs.label: Ngari virus is a Bunyamwera virus reassortant that can be associated with large outbreaks of hemorrhagic fever in Africa. J Virol 2004

geo.text: Sub-Saharan Africa; Xingu virus in South America.

profile.headline: North American Bunyamwera-serogroup virus; a teratogen in sheep and a rare cause of severe human neuroinvasive disease.
profile.syndrome: Rare but documented human meningoencephalitis and multi-organ disease, including fatal cases; mild febrile illness is likely far more common. In sheep, it causes abortion and congenital malformation.
profile.transmission: Many mosquito species; white-tailed deer and other cervids amplify.
profile.geography: North and Central America.
profile.diagnosis: CSF/serum serology and RT-PCR at reference laboratories.
evidence: Several well-documented human neuroinvasive and fatal cases confirmed virologically in the US and Canada.

refs.label: Second human case of Cache Valley virus disease. Emerg Infect Dis 2006
Cache valley virus in a patient diagnosed with aseptic meningitis. J Clin Microbiol 2013

geo.text: North and Central America.

profile.headline: Newly characterised Bunyamwera-serogroup virus from Xinjiang, China; studied alongside Oya virus as an emerging orthobunyavirus of concern.
profile.syndrome: No confirmed human disease to date. Pathogenic in mice and competent for transmission by Culex pipiens pallens.
profile.transmission: Culex mosquitoes.
profile.reservoir: Not established; detected in mosquitoes and ticks.
profile.geography: Northwestern China (Ebinur Lake, Xinjiang).
profile.diagnosis: Specific RT-qPCR (95% LOD ~0.37 PFU/mL).
evidence: Culex pipiens pallens showed a transmission rate up to 15.4% with 3.3% transmission efficiency in oral-infection experiments — true vector competence, unlike for Oya virus.
Shares the AhR–CYP1A1 interferon-evasion mechanism with Oya virus.

geo.text: Northwestern China (Ebinur Lake, Xinjiang).
